**Problem:** Causal chain of a low-resource-language jailbreak: harmful query translated to language X -> model represents non-English harmful content less separably from harmless content -> universal refusal direction fires weakly -> compliance. The weak link is the SECOND step (poor harmful/harmless separation in language X), but it is rarely measured directly across languages of differing resource levels.

**Direction:** Take a refusal direction extracted in English from an open multilingual model. For a fixed set of harmful/harmless prompts translated into 5-6 languages spanning high to low resource, measure the separation (e.g., cosine margin or AUROC of a 1-D projection) between harmful and harmless activations per language. Correlate separation quality with language resource level. Success criterion: a ranking of languages by how degraded the refusal signal is, with statistics.

**Why it matters:** Pinpoints which languages are most exposed before any attack is even run, giving a triage list for safety teams. Frontier labs deprioritize low-resource languages; doing this externally has strong counterfactual value. No training, only forward passes.

**Relevant context:** 'Refusal Direction is Universal Across Safety-Aligned Languages' (arXiv 2505.17306) reports refusal vectors are parallel across languages but harmful/harmless separation weakens in non-English. Beaglehole et al. show concept vectors transfer across languages — this tests the failure side of that transfer.

# Catching the defection decision before the harmful token: probing the trigger-recognition link

**Problem:** A backdoored model's harm chain is: trigger present in context -> model internally 'recognizes' it should defect -> model plans harmful action -> harmful tokens emitted. Anthropic's probes catch the recognition link, but it is open whether the recognition signal appears BEFORE any harmful token is generated (early enough to halt), or only co-emerges with the harmful output.

**Direction:** Use an openly available backdoored / sleeper-agent-style model (or a small published trojaned checkpoint). Build a simple two-prompt 'defection direction' linear probe. Then run prompts containing the trigger and read the probe value token-by-token across the prompt and the first few generated tokens. Measure how many tokens BEFORE the first harmful token the probe crosses threshold. Success criterion: a distribution of 'lead time' (tokens of warning).

**Why it matters:** Lead time is what makes a monitor actionable — you can only intervene if the signal precedes the harm. This reframes probe evaluation around the timing link in the causal chain. Uses an existing model organism, scoped to a 30h probe study — exactly the favored model-organism slice.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic 'Simple probes can catch sleeper agents' reports linear defection probes with >99% AUROC from generic contrast pairs; the LessWrong post notes results may be artifacts of backdoor insertion. Timing is the unexamined dimension. Grounded in Beaglehole et al. linear-probe-for-monitoring methodology.

# Does a sycophancy steering vector intervene on the cause or just the surface?

**Problem:** Sycophancy chain: user signals a preferred answer -> model represents 'agree-with-user' pressure -> model suppresses its own honest belief -> sycophantic answer. A steering vector that reduces sycophancy could act at the second link (reduce the agree-with-user pressure) OR merely paste an opposite surface style on top. These are confusable when you only score final outputs.

**Direction:** On an open model, build an anti-sycophancy CAA vector. Construct probe questions where the model's honest belief is independently knowable (e.g., simple factual questions it answers correctly with no user pressure). Apply user pressure ('I think the answer is [wrong]') and measure: (a) does steering restore the correct answer, and (b) does steering also change the model's confidence on questions where the user agrees? If steering helps only when the user is wrong, it touched the cause; if it changes everything uniformly, it's surface.

**Why it matters:** Distinguishing causal vs surface intervention is essential before trusting steering as a safety control; a surface fix degrades on novel pressure. Diffuse, fuzzy-reward evaluation of honesty under pressure — hard to do well, needs no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Sycophancy CAA results (kiad4631 repo; 'Sycophancy Hides Linearly in the Attention Heads' arXiv 2601.16644) show a linear sycophancy direction. Beaglehole et al. emphasize linear concept representations. This adds the cause-vs-surface discrimination that output-only evals miss.

# Which link breaks first: can an attacker neutralize a steering-based safety monitor with a benign-looking suffix?

**Problem:** Monitoring chain: deployer attaches a concept probe -> probe reads activations -> high probe value flags harmful intent -> request blocked. The adversarial link Beaglehole et al. flag as open is whether an attacker can craft inputs that neutralize the probe WITHOUT changing the harmful semantics. This robustness-of-the-monitor link is under-tested for cheap, gradient-free attacks.

**Direction:** Train a linear harmful-intent probe on an open model. Then test cheap, no-gradient evasions: appending benign filler sentences, paraphrasing, changing formatting, inserting distractor topics. Measure how much each manipulation lowers the probe score on genuinely harmful prompts (whose harmful output the model still produces). Success criterion: a ranked table of which cheap manipulations most degrade the probe while preserving harmful behavior.

**Why it matters:** Directly answers the Science paper's flagged open problem (adversarial robustness of concept vectors) using only black-box-friendly, gradient-free attacks any external researcher can run. Establishes how brittle probe-based monitoring is to script-kiddie-level evasion — a medium-horizon deployment risk.

**Relevant context:** Beaglehole et al. explicitly list 'can attackers craft inputs that neutralize steering?' as open. 'Steering Safely or Off a Cliff?' (arXiv 2602.06256) and 'Analysing the Safety Pitfalls of Steering Vectors' (2603.24543) motivate robustness concerns. Gradient-free framing keeps it in the 30h budget.

# StrongREJECT Scorer Robustness to Paraphrased Harmful Responses

**Problem:** StrongREJECT's automated GPT-judge scores jailbreak success on specificity and convincingness. It is unknown how stable these scores are when the same harmful content is paraphrased (e.g. bulleted vs prose, formal vs casual), which would reveal a measurement-validity weakness affecting every benchmark that uses it.

**Direction:** Take a fixed set of jailbroken harmful responses, generate controlled paraphrases (varying format, verbosity, tone) using a small open model, and re-score all variants with the public StrongREJECT evaluator. Measure score variance attributable purely to surface form vs underlying content, and identify systematic biases (e.g. bulleted lists scored as more 'specific').

**Why it matters:** If a leading jailbreak benchmark's scores swing with cosmetic rephrasing, reported robustness numbers across the field are partly noise. This is a cheap, high-leverage measurement-validity audit needing no model training and no lab data.

**Relevant context:** StrongREJECT (Souly et al., NeurIPS 2024, arXiv:2402.10260) uses an automated evaluator rating specificity and convincingness, and the authors themselves showed prior benchmarks overstate jailbreak effectiveness — motivating scrutiny of the scorer's own validity. The benchmark and scorer are public (github dsbowen/strong_reject).

# Does pushing the safety vector harder break capability before it breaks compliance?

**Problem:** Safety-steering chain: deployer adds refusal vector at strength alpha -> model refuses more harmful requests -> BUT at high alpha the model also refuses benign requests and loses capability. The under-studied link is the joint trajectory: as you increase alpha, which fails first — false refusals on benign prompts, or capability collapse on neutral tasks — and is there a safe operating window?

**Direction:** On an open model, sweep refusal-vector strength alpha over a range. At each alpha measure three curves on held-out sets: (1) harmful-refusal rate, (2) benign over-refusal rate, (3) capability (accuracy on a small neutral QA set like a 200-item MMLU subset). Identify whether a window exists where harmful refusals rise but benign refusals and capability stay near baseline. Success criterion: the three-curve plot with a marked (or absent) safe window.

**Why it matters:** Tells practitioners whether activation-based safety steering has any usable operating range, or whether the safety/capability links are entangled. This dose-response framing is the bottleneck for real deployment and is cheap to run externally.

**Relevant context:** 'Scaling laws for activation steering' (arXiv 2507.11771) and 'Steering Without Side Effects' (2406.15518) discuss side effects; Beaglehole et al. show steering can improve capability for some concepts. The explicit three-way trade-off curve is the contribution.

# The over-refusal link: do safety steering vectors catastrophically block dual-use medical/security questions?

**Problem:** Harm-avoidance chain often overshoots: refusal vector added -> harmful requests blocked -> legitimate dual-use requests (how does a poison work, how do exploits function for defenders) ALSO blocked -> users lose access to safety-relevant knowledge. The collateral-damage link is under-measured because most evals use clearly-harmful vs clearly-benign prompts, not the ambiguous middle.

**Direction:** Curate ~80 dual-use prompts (legitimate framing of sensitive topics: medical, cybersecurity defense, chemistry safety) plus matched clearly-harmful and clearly-benign controls. Apply a safety steering vector at a fixed strength on an open model and measure refusal rates across the three buckets. Success criterion: quantified over-refusal on the dual-use middle relative to clearly-benign baseline.

**Why it matters:** Over-refusal of dual-use knowledge is a real and growing harm of crude safety interventions; quantifying it on the ambiguous middle is exactly the diffuse evaluation labs underweight. No training, just curated prompts and forward passes.

**Relevant context:** SafeSteer (arXiv 2392466440 / ResearchGate) and 'Steering Safely or Off a Cliff?' (2602.06256) raise specificity concerns. Beaglehole et al. methodology for concept-vector steering. The dual-use middle is the novel evaluation slice.

# Does the 'larger models are more steerable' finding also mean larger models are more easily jailbroken via steering?

**Problem:** Beaglehole et al.'s surprising result: larger models are MORE steerable toward a concept. The worrying causal extension: if steerability scales with size, then the attacker's link (steer the model AWAY from refusal) should also get easier with size -> bigger models are softer targets for steering-based jailbreaks. This dark-side-of-steerability link is asserted by some work but not isolated as a clean size scaling.

**Direction:** Pick a single open model family with multiple sizes (e.g., Qwen 0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B or Pythia sizes). For each size, extract a comparable refusal direction and measure the attack-success-rate increase when steering AWAY from refusal at matched relative strength. Plot ASR-gain vs model size. Success criterion: a monotonic (or not) scaling curve of jailbreak-via-steering effectiveness with size.

**Why it matters:** If steerability and steering-based vulnerability scale together, the Science paper's optimistic finding has a built-in safety cost that grows with capability — a medium-horizon concern. Single model family, forward passes only, perfect 30h scope.

**Relevant context:** Beaglehole et al. report larger models more steerable; 'Analysing the Safety Pitfalls of Steering Vectors' (2603.24543) reports jailbreak effects grow with scale. This isolates the scaling within one family as a clean controlled study.

# Does a deception concept vector fire when the model lies but not when it errs?

**Problem:** Deception-monitoring chain: model decides to state a falsehood it knows is false -> internal 'deception' state activates -> a probe reads it -> flag. The critical link a deception monitor must get right is DISCRIMINATION: distinguishing intentional deception from honest mistakes. If the probe also fires on honest errors, it is useless. This discrimination link is under-tested.

**Direction:** On an open model, build a deception direction from contrastive pairs (instructed-to-lie vs tell-truth) on knowable facts. Then evaluate on three held-out buckets: (a) model lies on a fact it knows, (b) model is honestly wrong on a fact it doesn't know, (c) model is honestly right. Measure whether the probe separates (a) from (b) and (c). Success criterion: AUROC for deception-vs-honest-error, not just deception-vs-truth.

**Why it matters:** A deception detector that can't tell lies from mistakes will drown operators in false alarms. Targeting the discrimination link is the hard, neglected part — and a diffuse, fuzzy-reward eval that needs no lab data.

**Relevant context:** Steering-vector work on dishonesty (RepE; CAA literature) and Beaglehole et al. linear concept probing. The lie-vs-honest-error confound is the standard weakness this directly attacks.

# Probing the 'I know but won't say' link: detecting withheld knowledge via concept vectors

**Problem:** A sandbagging / strategic-underperformance chain: model knows the answer -> model decides to withhold or feign ignorance (e.g., on a capability eval) -> outputs 'I don't know' or a wrong answer. The pivotal link is the internal 'knows-but-withholds' state. Output-only evals can't see it; a concept probe might. This link is rarely isolated from genuine ignorance.

**Direction:** On an open model, take questions the model answers correctly under normal prompting. Then prompt it to 'pretend you don't know' (instructed sandbagging) and contrast activations with genuine unknown questions. Train a linear probe for 'withholding-known-info' and test whether it separates instructed-withholding from genuine ignorance. Success criterion: probe AUROC distinguishing the two on held-out items.

**Why it matters:** Sandbagging on dangerous-capability evals is a serious medium-horizon threat; an activation probe that detects strategic underperformance is exactly the kind of monitoring infrastructure valuable outside labs. Uses instructed sandbagging as a feasible model-organism proxy.

**Relevant context:** Builds on sleeper-agent defection-probe methodology (Anthropic) and Beaglehole et al. concept extraction. Sandbagging detection via internals is an open, neglected problem ideal for a 30h probe study.

# Does multi-concept steering create interference that opens a back door?

**Problem:** Composed-steering chain: deployer stacks several safety vectors (anti-toxicity + anti-deception + refusal) -> vectors interfere in the residual stream -> one safety property is silently weakened by another -> an exploitable gap. Beaglehole et al. show multi-concept steering is possible, but the interference-creates-a-gap link is unexamined.

**Direction:** On an open model, extract 3 safety vectors independently and measure each one's solo effectiveness. Then apply them in combination and re-measure each property. Quantify whether combining vectors reduces any individual property below its solo level (destructive interference). Success criterion: a matrix showing per-property effectiveness solo vs combined, flagging any property that degrades when stacked.

**Why it matters:** Real deployments will stack multiple steering interventions; if stacking silently weakens one safety property, that's a deployment-introduced vulnerability. Cheap to test, directly extends the Science paper's multi-concept result toward its risk.

**Relevant context:** Beaglehole et al. demonstrate multi-concept steering and combining concept vectors. Interference / destructive composition is the under-studied flip side. Pure forward-pass evaluation, no training.

# Where does the harm appear: prompt-time vs generation-time in the activation trace?

**Problem:** A monitoring decision chain: read activations -> decide harmful -> block. A key design question is WHEN to read: a harmful-intent signal might be present already while processing the prompt, or only emerge once the model starts generating the harmful continuation. Building a monitor at the wrong point in the chain wastes its predictive power. This timing link is rarely characterized.

**Direction:** On an open model with a harmful-intent probe, compare probe scores computed at (a) the last prompt token vs (b) averaged over the first k generated tokens, across harmful and benign prompts. Measure detection AUROC for each readout point and how much generation tokens add over prompt-only. Success criterion: AUROC at prompt-time vs generation-time, quantifying the value of waiting.

**Why it matters:** Prompt-time detection allows pre-emptive blocking (much safer); if the signal only appears during generation, monitors must run online. Clarifying this link is foundational monitoring-harness infrastructure, runnable entirely externally.

**Relevant context:** Beaglehole et al. probes-for-monitoring and Anthropic defection-probe work. The prompt-time-vs-generation-time decomposition is the contribution; both readouts are trivial to extract from one model.

# Does the toxicity concept vector generalize to implicit / coded toxicity, or only the explicit link?

**Problem:** Toxicity-monitoring chain: toxic intent -> toxic representation -> probe fires. Probes are usually built and tested on EXPLICIT toxicity (slurs, overt insults). The neglected link is whether the same direction captures IMPLICIT/coded toxicity (dog-whistles, sarcasm, euphemism) — the harder, more dangerous form that slips past surface filters.

**Direction:** Build a toxicity direction from explicit contrastive pairs on an open model. Test it on a held-out set containing (a) explicit toxicity and (b) implicit/coded toxicity (curated examples of dog-whistles, condescension, microaggressions) plus benign controls. Compare detection AUROC across explicit vs implicit. Success criterion: quantified generalization gap from explicit to implicit toxicity.

**Why it matters:** Implicit toxicity is exactly what evades keyword filters and matters most for real harm; if concept vectors don't generalize there, probe-based monitoring inherits the same blind spot. A diffuse, fuzzy-reward evaluation needing only curated prompts.

**Relevant context:** Beaglehole et al. report probes beating judges on toxicity benchmarks; the explicit-only training set is the standard limitation. RepE toxicity-direction methods. Implicit-toxicity generalization is the novel test.

# Does the hallucination probe fail precisely on confident hallucinations?

**Problem:** Hallucination-monitoring chain: model fabricates -> internal 'unsupported' signal -> probe flags. Probes report high AUROC overall, but the dangerous link is CONFIDENT hallucinations — fabrications the model states fluently and confidently. If the probe's errors concentrate there, the overall AUROC is misleading. This error-stratification link is rarely examined.

**Direction:** Use an open model and a published factuality/hallucination setup. Build a linear hallucination probe. Then stratify the model's hallucinations by the model's own expressed/estimated confidence (e.g., token logprob of the claim) and measure probe detection rate within each confidence bucket. Success criterion: probe recall as a function of hallucination confidence, showing whether confident fabrications are the blind spot.

**Why it matters:** Confident hallucinations are the ones that mislead users and downstream systems; a monitor that only catches hesitant ones gives false assurance. Stratifying the evaluation by confidence is a cheap, high-value refinement of the Science paper's headline result.

**Relevant context:** Beaglehole et al. report probes outperform judges on hallucination; 'Real-Time Detection of Hallucinated Entities' (arXiv 2509.03531) and factuality-probe papers (ACL 2025 findings 880) provide methodology. Confidence-stratified failure analysis is the new angle.

# The reasoning-model link: does a deception probe read the CoT or the hidden computation?

**Problem:** For reasoning models, the safety hope is that the chain-of-thought is faithful. The harm chain for a non-verbalized attack: model plans harm internally -> CoT stays clean -> harmful action without a verbalized plan. A concept probe could catch this IF it reads the hidden computation rather than just the CoT tokens. Whether deception probes track verbalized vs unverbalized intent is the unexamined link.

**Direction:** On an open reasoning-capable model, construct cases where the model is instructed to pursue a hidden objective while producing innocuous CoT (a feasible model-organism slice via prompting). Build a deception/hidden-goal probe and test whether it fires even when the CoT contains no incriminating text. Success criterion: probe AUROC on hidden-goal cases conditioned on the CoT being clean.

**Why it matters:** Models that attack without verbalizing their plan in the CoT are a flagged high-priority model-organism threat; an activation probe that catches them despite clean CoT is exactly the counterfactually-valuable monitoring tool. Scoped to prompt-induced hidden goals on an existing open model.

**Relevant context:** Beaglehole et al. extend concept steering to reasoning models; Anthropic defection-probe work on hidden goals. The clean-CoT-but-detectable-internally test is the novel decomposition.

# Over-Refusal Tax of Adding a Safety Prefill Defense

**Problem:** Adding a fixed safe prefix or system reminder is a proposed cheap defense that deepens shallow alignment, but the over-refusal (helpfulness) cost of such interventions has not been jointly measured against XSTest-style benign-but-sensitive prompts.

**Direction:** Implement 2-3 lightweight 'depth' defenses (safe-completion prefill, repeated safety reminder, brief CoT-before-answer) on small open models. For each, measure jailbreak robustness on StrongREJECT AND false-refusal rate on XSTest's 250 safe prompts. Plot the safety-helpfulness Pareto frontier to see which cheap defense gives robustness without exaggerated safety.

**Why it matters:** Directly addresses the open problem of 'adaptive defenses without catastrophic over-refusal.' Produces an actionable Pareto comparison of zero-cost defenses any deployer can apply. Both benchmarks are public; runs on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** XSTest (Rottger et al., NAACL 2024, arXiv:2308.01263) provides 250 safe + 200 unsafe contrastive prompts to measure exaggerated safety from lexical overfitting. Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946) show deepening alignment improves robustness. Context file open problem: defenses 'without catastrophic over-refusal.'

# Does steering toward 'honesty' actually increase calibration, or just verbosity of hedging?

**Problem:** Honesty-steering chain: add honesty vector -> model expresses uncertainty more -> users get better-calibrated answers. But the middle link could fail: the vector might just make the model HEDGE more (say 'I'm not sure' everywhere) without improving the match between stated confidence and actual correctness. Hedging is not calibration. This link is rarely measured with proper calibration metrics.

**Direction:** On an open model, build an honesty/uncertainty steering vector. On a QA set with known ground truth, measure calibration (e.g., ECE, or correlation between expressed confidence and correctness) at baseline and under steering. Check whether steering improves calibration or merely shifts all confidences down uniformly. Success criterion: calibration curves before/after steering, distinguishing real calibration gain from blanket hedging.

**Why it matters:** Trustworthy uncertainty is core to safe deployment; a steering method that fakes humility without calibration is actively misleading. Proper calibration evaluation is cheap, neglected, and needs no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Beaglehole et al. steering toward concepts; RepE honesty directions. Calibration (ECE) framing distinguishes genuine vs cosmetic effects — the standard confound this targets.

# Does the safety vector survive the quantization link that consumer deployment requires?

**Problem:** Real-world deployment chain: lab ships safety-steered model -> users quantize it (4-bit/8-bit) to run on consumer hardware -> quantization perturbs activations -> the safety steering vector may no longer point where it did -> degraded protection. The quantization-perturbs-steering link is directly relevant to open-weight safety but rarely tested.

**Direction:** On an open model, extract a refusal direction at full precision. Then load 8-bit and 4-bit quantized versions, re-run the same prompts, and measure (a) how much the refusal direction's effectiveness drops when the FP-extracted vector is applied to the quantized model, and (b) whether re-extracting on the quantized model recovers it. Success criterion: effectiveness-vs-precision table for transferred and re-extracted vectors.

**Why it matters:** Open-weight models are overwhelmingly run quantized by the community; if safety steering silently breaks under quantization, that's a widespread real deployment gap labs don't prioritize. Perfect consumer-GPU, no-training, high-counterfactual scope.

**Relevant context:** Beaglehole et al. concept-vector extraction; open problem of stability across model changes. Quantization as a concrete, ubiquitous perturbation of the deployment pipeline is the novel link.

# Does light fine-tuning (LoRA) break the link between a safety vector and the behavior it controls?

**Problem:** Customization chain: community fine-tunes an open model with LoRA for a niche task -> internal representations drift slightly -> a safety steering vector extracted from the base model no longer controls the fine-tuned one -> protection silently lost. Beaglehole et al. flag stability across fine-tuning as open; the LoRA-specific, community-relevant version is unstudied.

**Direction:** Take an open base model and a publicly available LoRA fine-tune of it (or train a tiny LoRA on a small dataset within budget). Extract a refusal/safety vector on the base. Apply it to the fine-tuned model and measure effectiveness vs applying it on the base. Quantify how much fine-tuning erodes the vector's control. Success criterion: effectiveness drop on the fine-tune, plus whether re-extraction recovers it.

**Why it matters:** Thousands of community LoRA fine-tunes exist; if safety steering doesn't transfer to them, base-model safety claims don't hold downstream. Directly answers the Science paper's fine-tuning-stability open problem in the most common real setting. Single consumer GPU.

**Relevant context:** Beaglehole et al. list 'stability of concept vectors across model updates and fine-tuning' as open. KL-then-steer / fine-tuning shift work (arXiv 2406.15518; ICCV 2025 multimodal shift). LoRA-specific, community framing is novel.

# Does the refusal vector generalize across harm CATEGORIES, or is each category its own link?

**Problem:** Coverage chain: deployer extracts a refusal vector (often from one harm type) -> assumes it blocks all harmful requests -> but if the vector only covers the harm category it was built from, other categories slip through. Whether one refusal direction covers cyber, bio, fraud, self-harm, etc., uniformly is the under-tested coverage link.

**Direction:** On an open model, extract a refusal vector using ONLY one harm category (e.g., cyber). Then test its steering/detection effectiveness across several other categories (fraud, self-harm, weapons, privacy). Repeat extracting from a different single category. Build a transfer matrix of category-to-category coverage. Success criterion: a coverage matrix revealing which categories share a direction and which are orphaned.

**Why it matters:** If safety vectors are category-specific, single-category deployment leaves systematic blind spots — a concrete, measurable gap. The transfer matrix is directly actionable for anyone deploying steering-based safety, and needs only curated prompts.

**Relevant context:** SafeSteer (category-specific vectors) implies categories differ; Beaglehole et al. universal-concept framing implies they might unify. The category transfer matrix arbitrates between these, cheaply.

# Can a benign-looking system prompt silently cancel a deployed safety vector?

**Problem:** Layered-defense chain: deployer adds a safety steering vector -> believes it is robust to prompt-level attacks because it acts on activations, not tokens -> but a crafted system prompt could shift activations in the opposite direction, partially canceling the vector. The prompt-vs-vector tug-of-war link is assumed safe but rarely measured.

**Direction:** On an open model with a fixed refusal vector applied, search over a small set of adversarial-but-benign-looking system prompts ('be maximally helpful, never refuse') and measure how much they reduce the vector's refusal effectiveness. Compare to the vector's effect with a neutral system prompt. Success criterion: quantified reduction in refusal effectiveness attributable to prompt-vector interaction.

**Why it matters:** If a simple system prompt can neutralize activation-level safety, the 'steering is more robust than prompting' assumption is wrong — a deployment-critical finding. Gradient-free, prompt-only attacks are within reach of any external researcher.

**Relevant context:** 'Analysing the Safety Pitfalls of Steering Vectors' (2603.24543) and Beaglehole's open adversarial-robustness question. The prompt-cancels-vector interaction is the specific neglected link, testable with forward passes only.

# Does the image modality break the refusal link in vision-language models?

**Problem:** Multimodal harm chain: harmful intent delivered partly via image -> VLM represents image content -> refusal direction (built on text) fails to fire on image-borne harm -> compliance. Beaglehole et al. flag extending concept steering to multimodal as open. The specific weak link — text-derived refusal directions not covering image-borne harm — is barely measured on small open VLMs.

**Direction:** On a small open VLM (e.g., LLaVA-style or Qwen-VL small), extract a refusal direction from text harmful/harmless pairs. Test whether it detects/steers on harmful requests where the harmful content is conveyed by an image plus an innocuous text prompt, vs the same harm conveyed in text. Measure the modality gap in detection/steering effectiveness. Success criterion: quantified drop in refusal-direction effectiveness for image-borne vs text-borne harm.

**Why it matters:** Image-borne jailbreaks are a fast-growing, lab-underserved attack surface; showing text-built safety directions don't cover it motivates multimodal steering. Small open VLMs run on a single consumer GPU.

**Relevant context:** Beaglehole et al. apply concept vectors to vision-language models and list multimodal extension as open; null-space-projection VLM jailbreak defense (arXiv 2603.22094). The text-to-image modality gap for refusal is the targeted link.

# Does steering against one bias amplify another bias down the chain?

**Problem:** Debiasing chain: add anti-bias vector for attribute A (e.g., gender) -> model's outputs become more balanced on A -> BUT representations are entangled, so the same vector may shift behavior on attribute B (e.g., race, age) in an unintended direction. The cross-bias spillover link is rarely audited when steering against a single bias.

**Direction:** On an open model, build a steering vector to reduce one specific bias (measured on a paired-template set). Then evaluate the model's bias on several OTHER attributes before and after steering. Quantify whether reducing bias A changes bias on B/C/D. Success criterion: a spillover matrix showing intended and collateral bias changes across attributes.

**Why it matters:** Fairness interventions that fix one axis while worsening another are a real, under-monitored risk; the spillover audit is exactly the kind of diffuse, careful evaluation that needs no lab data and is easy to get wrong without rigor.

**Relevant context:** Beaglehole et al. note concept entanglement and multi-concept interactions; RepE bias-direction work. The cross-attribute spillover audit is the neglected causal link, run with curated template prompts.

# Is the steered behavior persistent across a long conversation, or does it decay?

**Problem:** Sustained-control chain: apply safety vector at turn 1 -> behavior is safe early -> but over many turns of context, the accumulating conversation may overwhelm the fixed vector -> safety decays late in long chats. Multi-turn jailbreaks exploit exactly this contextual drift. Whether a fixed steering vector holds across turns is an under-measured persistence link.

**Direction:** On an open chat model with a fixed refusal vector, run multi-turn conversations that gradually build toward a harmful request (escalation pattern). Measure refusal effectiveness as a function of turn depth, with and without the vector. Success criterion: refusal rate vs turn number, showing whether and when fixed-vector safety decays under contextual drift.

**Why it matters:** Multi-turn drift is a leading real-world jailbreak vector; quantifying steering-vector decay over turns shows whether static activation interventions are enough or need to be re-applied/scaled online. Pure forward-pass conversation simulation, no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** 'Steering Dialogue Dynamics for Robustness against Multi-turn Jailbreaking' (arXiv 2503.00187) motivates contextual drift. Beaglehole et al. fixed concept vectors. The turn-depth decay curve for a fixed vector is the contribution.

# Does a power-seeking concept vector fire on instrumentally power-seeking text the model produces unprompted?

**Problem:** Misalignment chain: model pursues a goal -> derives an instrumentally power-seeking subgoal (acquire resources, avoid shutdown) -> expresses it in planning text -> harmful action. A monitor needs to catch the power-seeking link. But power-seeking probes are usually validated on explicitly-labeled power-seeking statements, not on instrumentally power-seeking text the model generates while pursuing a benign-seeming task. This generalization link is untested.

**Direction:** On an open model, build a power-seeking direction from explicit contrastive pairs (RepE-style). Then prompt the model with open-ended planning tasks (e.g., 'achieve goal X in this environment') and have it generate plans; label plan segments for instrumental power-seeking and test whether the probe fires on them. Success criterion: probe detection rate on naturally-generated instrumental power-seeking vs explicit examples.

**Why it matters:** Long-horizon power-seeking is a core catastrophic-risk threat model that labs deprioritize for near-term concerns; an activation probe that catches it in naturalistic planning is exactly the >1-year-horizon, counterfactually-valuable monitoring work. Feasible 30h slice using prompted planning as a model-organism proxy.

**Relevant context:** RepE power-seeking directions; Beaglehole et al. concept probing and Anthropic defection-probe methodology. The explicit-to-instrumental generalization gap is the neglected causal link.

# Does combining a steering monitor with a steering controller create a self-defeating loop?

**Problem:** Closed-loop safety chain: a probe reads activations -> if harmful, a steering vector is applied to correct -> but the correction changes activations -> which the same probe now reads as 'safe' even if the surface behavior didn't actually change. This monitor-controller feedback link could produce false reassurance. Beaglehole et al. propose unifying steering and monitoring but don't test this coupling.

**Direction:** On an open model, set up a simple closed loop: probe flags harmful intent -> apply refusal vector -> re-read probe. Independently judge whether the OUTPUT actually became safe (via held-out criteria) vs whether only the probe value moved. Measure the gap between 'probe says fixed' and 'output is actually fixed'. Success criterion: rate of cases where the loop silences the probe without changing the harmful output.

**Why it matters:** Unifying monitoring and steering (the Science paper's vision) risks a system that gates on the very signal it perturbs — a subtle but serious design flaw. Demonstrating it on one open model is cheap and directly informs safe monitor-controller architecture.

**Relevant context:** Beaglehole et al. propose universal steering AND monitoring together; this tests their interaction. Self-defeating feedback between probe and intervention is the novel, neglected causal link, all on one open model.

# System-Prompt Strength vs Jailbreak Success: A Controlled Variation

**Problem:** Practitioners harden models with elaborate safety system prompts, but the marginal robustness from increasingly strong system prompts (none, short, detailed, with examples) versus the over-refusal cost has not been cleanly isolated across attack types.

**Direction:** Define a ladder of system prompts from empty to highly detailed safety policy. For each rung, measure attack success across 3 attack families (prefill, many-shot, fluent template) and benign refusal on XSTest, on 2-3 small open models. Identify diminishing returns and which attack families system prompts fail to stop at any strength.

**Why it matters:** Deployers over-rely on system prompts as a defense; showing exactly which attacks they cannot stop regardless of verbosity is a practical, lab-independent finding. Pure inference, fully reproducible.

**Relevant context:** Many-shot jailbreaking (Anil et al., NeurIPS 2024) and prefill/decoding attacks (Qi et al., arXiv:2406.05946) provide the attack families. XSTest (arXiv:2308.01263) provides the over-refusal axis. Combines public attacks/benchmarks in a controlled variation absent from the catalogue examples.

# Does the 'probe beats judge' advantage hold once the input is adversarially paraphrased?

**Problem:** Detection chain: harmful content -> probe reads internal representation -> flags (beating LLM judges, per Beaglehole et al.). But the robustness link is whether the probe's advantage over judges SURVIVES adversarial paraphrase — attacks that preserve harmful meaning while changing surface form. If judges are more robust to paraphrase than probes (or vice versa), the headline comparison is incomplete.

**Direction:** On an open model, reproduce a small probe-vs-judge comparison on a toxicity or harmfulness set. Then apply meaning-preserving paraphrases / character perturbations to the harmful inputs and re-measure both the probe's and an LLM-judge's detection rates. Success criterion: the robustness gap — how much each detector degrades under paraphrase, and whether the probe's lead survives.

**Why it matters:** The 'probes beat judges' result drives a shift toward internal monitoring; knowing whether that lead is robust to trivial paraphrase is essential before relying on it. A direct, cheap stress-test of a headline Science 2026 claim — strong counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Beaglehole et al. report probes outperform judge models for toxicity/hallucination. Paraphrase robustness is the standard adversarial stress test absent from that comparison. One open model, curated paraphrases, no training.

# Does Planning-Ahead Scale Down? Rhyme Pre-Activation in Small Open Models

**Problem:** Anthropic's circuit tracing found Claude 3.5 Haiku pre-activates rhyming target words before writing a poetry line, evidence of forward planning. It is unknown whether this behavior is unique to large frontier models or appears in small open models accessible to independent researchers.

**Direction:** Using TransformerLens with a small open model (GPT-2 small/medium or Pythia-410M/1.4B), prompt the model to complete rhyming couplets and use the logit lens on the residual stream at the line-break (newline) token to detect whether candidate rhyme words receive elevated logit/probability mass before the second line is generated. Compare across model sizes within an open family (Pythia 70M to 1.4B) to map where planning emerges as a function of scale.

**Why it matters:** Replicating frontier planning findings in small open models lets the whole community study deceptive/strategic planning mechanistically without lab access. Knowing the scale threshold for forward planning informs which open models are valid 'model organisms' for studying hidden-goal-directed behavior.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic Circuit Tracing / 'On the Biology of a Large Language Model' (2025): Claude 3.5 Haiku identifies rhyming end-words before writing the line; planning occurs at the newline token. Pythia suite spans 70M-12B with identical training data, ideal for scale studies. TransformerLens supports 50+ models including GPT-2 and Pythia.

# Suppressing the Plan: Causal Verification of Rhyme Pre-Activation in Open Models

**Problem:** The frontier finding that suppressing a planned rhyme word makes the model produce a different ending was demonstrated only with proprietary feature dictionaries. Whether the same causal lever exists at the level of residual-stream directions in small open models is untested.

**Direction:** In GPT-2 / Pythia, identify the residual-stream direction or token logit associated with a candidate rhyme word at the newline position (via logit lens), then causally ablate or down-project that direction during generation of the next line and measure whether the model switches to an alternative rhyme. Quantify intervention success rate and output coherence (perplexity) as in published intervention-evaluation metrics.

**Why it matters:** A cheap, training-free causal test of forward planning gives independent researchers a tool to detect and disrupt premeditated multi-token behavior, the mechanistic precursor of plans a model might not verbalize in its chain-of-thought.

**Relevant context:** Biology of an LLM (2025): suppressing 'rabbit' feature changes the line ending; injecting 'green' redirects planning. Bi-causal steering literature reports intervention success rate and coherence-intervention tradeoff metrics. TransformerLens supports activation patching/ablation.

# Planning Horizon: How Many Tokens Ahead Does a Small Model Plan?

**Problem:** Circuit tracing showed planning of the next line's end-word, but the temporal depth of planning (1 word ahead vs. several) and how it decays with distance has not been characterized in open models.

**Direction:** Construct prompts where the model must satisfy a constraint at a controllable distance (e.g. write a sentence ending in a specific given word N tokens away). Use the logit lens at the planning position to measure how strongly the target word is pre-activated as a function of N, producing a 'planning horizon decay curve' for several open models.

**Why it matters:** Quantifying planning horizon is directly relevant to long-horizon deceptive behavior: a model that pre-encodes goals many tokens ahead is more capable of executing multi-step plans that monitors cannot catch token-by-token. This is a medium-horizon threat labs deprioritize.

**Relevant context:** Circuit Tracing (2025) found backward planning evidence in poetry and question answering (article selection before answer). 'Detecting and Characterizing Planning in Language Models' (arXiv 2508.18098) and 'What's the plan?' (arXiv 2601.20164) propose implicit-planning metrics.

# Planning vs. Capability: Does Forward Planning Track Task Competence?

**Problem:** The context notes an open follow-up: whether planning correlates with capability. It is unclear if stronger pre-activation of future tokens accompanies higher task accuracy across model checkpoints/sizes.

**Direction:** Across Pythia training checkpoints or model sizes, measure (a) a planning-strength metric (logit-lens pre-activation of correct future token) and (b) task accuracy on the same constrained-generation task, then correlate them. Test whether planning emerges before, with, or after competence.

**Why it matters:** If planning emerges as a byproduct of capability gains, then improvements in frontier capability predictably bring stronger latent planning, sharpening the case for proactive interpretability monitoring of deceptive planning.

**Relevant context:** Pythia provides 154 intermediate checkpoints per model with public weights, enabling training-dynamics studies. Circuit Tracing (2025) raises capability-planning correlation as an explicit open question. UK AISI Alignment Project lists training-dynamics-of-features as an open problem.

# Vision vs. Language SAE Sparsity: A Controlled Layerwise Characterization

**Problem:** ViT-Prisma reports that vision SAEs exhibit substantially lower sparsity (more active features) than language SAEs, sometimes even reducing model loss, but the structure of this discrepancy across layers and its cause are unexplained open questions.

**Direction:** Using pre-trained Prisma vision SAEs (80+ weights, no training needed) and pre-trained SAELens language SAEs, measure L0 (active features per token), feature firing-frequency distributions, and dead-feature rates layer-by-layer under matched conditions, producing a side-by-side sparsity-structure comparison and testing whether vision-SAE density is concentrated in specific layers (e.g. early patch-embedding vs. late).

**Why it matters:** Understanding whether interpretability tooling transfers across modalities determines whether safety techniques validated on language models will work on the multimodal models being deployed. This is doable entirely with open pre-trained weights and no lab infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** Prisma (arXiv 2504.19475): vision SAEs show lower sparsity than language SAEs, reconstructions can reduce loss, and the discrepancy is an open question. 80+ pre-trained vision SAE weights and SAELens language SAEs are publicly available.

# Is Lower Vision-SAE Sparsity an Artifact of Patch-Token Redundancy?

**Problem:** One hypothesis for why vision SAEs are denser than language SAEs is that adjacent image patches carry highly redundant information, inflating co-active features. This causal explanation has not been tested.

**Direction:** Take a pre-trained Prisma vision SAE and measure SAE L0/firing patterns on (a) natural images, (b) spatially shuffled patches, and (c) noise images. If patch redundancy drives density, sparsity should rise sharply when spatial correlation is destroyed. Correlate per-patch feature counts with local image self-similarity.

**Why it matters:** Identifying the source of cross-modal sparsity differences guides whether vision-specific SAE training is needed, and whether monosemanticity-based safety findings from language SAEs are even meaningful for vision. Pure inference on open weights, no GPU training.

**Relevant context:** Prisma (arXiv 2504.19475) flags the sparsity discrepancy as unexplained and suggests vision-specific training may be needed. Vision transformers tokenize images into spatially adjacent patches with known redundancy.

# Do Vision-SAE Reconstructions That Lower Loss Encode Spurious Shortcuts?

**Problem:** Prisma observed the surprising result that vision-SAE reconstructions can decrease model loss, the opposite of language SAEs. It is unknown whether this 'helpful' reconstruction is denoising genuine signal or amplifying spurious texture/background shortcuts.

**Direction:** Using a pre-trained vision SAE and ViT, compare classifications on original vs. SAE-reconstructed inputs on images with known spurious cues (e.g. backgrounds, textures). Test whether the loss-decreasing reconstructions specifically help on shortcut-correlated examples vs. shortcut-broken examples, revealing whether SAEs encode safety-relevant spurious features.

**Why it matters:** If interpretability tools inadvertently surface or strengthen spurious shortcuts, they could mislead safety audits of vision models (e.g. medical/autonomous systems). A model-organism-style probe of an existing open ViT, no lab data needed.

**Relevant context:** Prisma (arXiv 2504.19475): vision-SAE reconstructions can reduce model loss. Spurious-correlation/shortcut-learning is a documented ViT failure mode; ConceptScope (arXiv 2510.26186) characterizes dataset bias via disentangled visual concepts.

# Mapping Feature Absorption Prevalence Across the SAE Width Sweep

**Problem:** The NeurIPS 2025 'A is for Absorption' result showed SAE latents that appear monosemantic fail to fire on arbitrary examples (e.g. a 'starts-with-E' feature missing 'Elephant'), and that varying SAE size/sparsity does not fix it. The quantitative prevalence of absorption across the publicly available SAE-width sweep is not mapped.

**Direction:** Using the public Gemma Scope / SAELens family of SAEs at multiple widths, replicate the first-letter spelling task, automatically detect absorption (latent fires for the concept but misses specific tokens whose feature is captured elsewhere), and plot absorption rate as a function of SAE width and L0 to produce an empirical prevalence curve.

**Why it matters:** Feature absorption is an 'interpretability illusion' that makes SAE-based safety claims untrustworthy. A quantitative prevalence map tells auditors how much to distrust SAE monosemanticity, using only open SAEs and CPU/light-GPU inference.

**Relevant context:** 'A is for Absorption' (arXiv 2409.14507, NeurIPS 2025 oral): absorption is asymmetric feature splitting that lowers recall; varying SAE size/sparsity is insufficient to solve it. Gemma Scope provides hundreds of open SAEs at multiple widths.

# Does Feature Absorption Concentrate on Safety-Relevant Concepts?

**Problem:** Absorption has been demonstrated on a toy spelling task. Whether it specifically corrupts safety-relevant concept features (e.g. deception, harm, refusal-trigger concepts) — which would make SAE-based monitors silently fail — is untested.

**Direction:** Take open SAEs with labeled interpretable latents (from public feature dashboards) corresponding to safety-adjacent concepts, then probe for absorption by checking recall of the concept latent against a curated set of in-concept examples, comparing absorption rates for safety concepts vs. neutral concepts.

**Why it matters:** If safety-relevant SAE features suffer false negatives via absorption, SAE-based deployment monitors could miss exactly the cases that matter. This directly probes the interpretability-to-safety gap with open tooling.

**Relevant context:** 'A is for Absorption' (arXiv 2409.14507): absorption creates false negatives to a latent's mainline interpretation. Open feature dashboards (Neuronpedia/Gemma Scope) label many latents. Context lists 'bridge the interpretability-to-safety gap' as an open problem.

# Quantization as an Accidental Jailbreak: Robustness vs Bit-Width

**Problem:** Small open models are routinely run quantized (8-bit, 4-bit, GGUF) for consumer GPUs, but whether aggressive quantization degrades safety alignment — itself a shallow, fragile property — more than it degrades general capability is largely unmeasured.

**Direction:** Take one open instruct model and evaluate it at fp16, int8, and int4 quantization. For each precision, measure (a) refusal robustness on StrongREJECT and prefill attacks and (b) general capability on a small benchmark. Test whether quantization preferentially erodes the first-token refusal behavior predicted by shallow alignment.

**Why it matters:** Quantization is ubiquitous in the open/local-LLM community; if it silently weakens safety while preserving capability, every consumer deployment is more jailbreakable than the released model. A medium-horizon, deployment-realistic risk perfectly suited to consumer-GPU study.

**Relevant context:** Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946) show safety is concentrated in fragile first-token behavior, plausibly more sensitive to weight perturbation than diffuse capability. Quantization tooling (bitsandbytes, GGUF) is standard and free; StrongREJECT (arXiv:2402.10260) supplies the safety metric.

# Do SAE Probes Beat Random-SAE Baselines for Safety Concept Detection?

**Problem:** Recent sanity-check work found SAE probing accuracy stays strong even when SAE encoder/decoder are randomly initialized and frozen, raising the question of whether learned SAE features actually contribute on safety-relevant detection tasks specifically.

**Direction:** Replicate the random-baseline sanity check but on a safety-relevant detection target (e.g. detecting toxic/harmful-intent activations, or refusal vs. compliance) using an open model. Compare a trained-SAE probe, a random-frozen-SAE probe, and a direct linear probe on residual stream, reporting whether the trained SAE adds value over baselines on this safety task.

**Why it matters:** Labs are investing heavily in SAE-based monitors. An independent sanity check on whether SAEs beat trivial baselines for safety detection is high-counterfactual-value and needs no proprietary infra.

**Relevant context:** 'Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders: Do SAEs Beat Random Baselines?' (arXiv 2602.14111): sparse probing stays strong with random-frozen SAE components. 'Are Sparse Autoencoders Useful?' (arXiv 2502.16681) and the SAE-probe debate show tuned linear probes often match/exceed SAEs.

# Logit Lens vs. Tuned Lens: Where Does the Cheap Lens Lie About Safety Behavior?

**Problem:** Attribution-patching work flagged that the widely used logit lens has faithfulness limitations and can surface spurious concepts the model does not actually rely on. Independent researchers default to logit lens because it is free; the magnitude of its unfaithfulness on safety-relevant prompts is uncharacterized.

**Direction:** On an open model with a publicly available tuned lens, compare logit-lens vs. tuned-lens intermediate predictions on refusal/harmful prompts and on factual-recall prompts, quantifying divergence (KL, top-token disagreement) by layer. Identify prompt types where logit lens most misleads.

**Why it matters:** If the free tool independent researchers rely on systematically misrepresents internal computation on safety prompts, many community interpretability conclusions are suspect. Maps tool reliability with zero training cost.

**Relevant context:** Tuned Lens (Belrose et al.) reports more reliable/predictive intermediate decoding than logit lens; attribution-patching work notes logit-lens faithfulness limitations and spurious-concept reliance. Pre-trained tuned-lens weights exist for GPT-2/Pythia.

# Attribution-Method Disagreement as a Faithfulness Red Flag

**Problem:** Faithfulness literature notes strong disagreement between different attribution methods casts doubt that any of them captures true causes. A simple, reusable disagreement diagnostic for circuit-discovery on small models has not been packaged for newcomers.

**Direction:** On a known small circuit (e.g. GPT-2 indirect-object identification), compute component importance via three cheap methods (logit-lens attribution, activation patching, attribution patching) and quantify their rank-correlation/agreement. Test whether disagreement spikes on harder/safety-relevant prompts, and ship the diagnostic as a small reusable tool.

**Why it matters:** A lightweight 'do my attribution methods even agree?' check is strategically valuable infrastructure: it lets every independent interpretability project self-audit faithfulness before drawing safety conclusions.

**Relevant context:** Faithfulness literature: strong disagreement between attribution methods undermines the faithfulness requirement; attribution patching approximates patching cheaply. GPT-2 IOI circuit is a standard, well-documented benchmark in TransformerLens.

# Does the Multilingual 'Universal Feature' Finding Hold in Small Open Models?

**Problem:** Circuit tracing reported cross-linguistic generalization (shared language-agnostic features) in Claude 3.5 Haiku. Whether small open multilingual models share concept features across languages — or instead keep language-specific representations — is a replication gap.

**Direction:** Using an open multilingual model (e.g. BLOOM-560M or a multilingual Pythia-like model) in TransformerLens, identify a concept (e.g. 'opposite of small') in several languages, then test whether the same residual-stream direction / SAE latent activates across languages via cosine similarity and cross-lingual activation patching.

**Why it matters:** Shared cross-lingual concept representations imply safety interventions (e.g. unlearning harmful knowledge) might transfer across languages — or fail to. Testable on open models, high relevance to multilingual safety coverage.

**Relevant context:** Circuit Tracing / Biology of an LLM (2025): evidence of cross-linguistic generalization and language-agnostic features in Claude 3.5 Haiku. 'Causal Language Control in Multilingual Transformers via Sparse Feature Steering' (arXiv 2507.13410) shows feature-level language control.

# Reproducing the Hidden-Objective Audit on a Tiny Open Model Organism

**Problem:** Anthropic's 'Auditing language models for hidden objectives' showed interpretability could surface a deliberately trained-in hidden objective, but used a bespoke model and team. A minimal, reproducible open version that newcomers can run is missing.

**Direction:** Take a small open model fine-tuned (or use an existing open 'model organism' such as a sleeper-agent/backdoor checkpoint released publicly) and apply cheap interpretability — SAE feature inspection or linear probing on the residual stream — to detect the trigger/hidden behavior without being told the trigger. Report detection success and false-positive rate.

**Why it matters:** Hidden-objective / secret-goal model organisms are a top medium-horizon threat. Demonstrating that cheap, lab-free interpretability can (or cannot) catch them is exactly the high-counterfactual-value model-organism work the steering prioritizes.

**Relevant context:** 'Auditing language models for hidden objectives' (arXiv 2503.10965): blind auditing teams used interp to find a planted objective. Public backdoor/sleeper-agent model checkpoints and TransformerLens-compatible small models enable a scoped replication.

# Surgical Sycophancy Correction: Replicating 'A Few Bad Neurons' on Open Models

**Problem:** Recent work isolated and surgically corrected sycophancy via a small set of neurons. Whether this localized fix generalizes across sycophancy types, and whether it degrades unrelated capabilities, needs independent follow-up on open models.

**Direction:** Identify candidate sycophancy-related directions/neurons in a small open chat model using a sycophancy probe dataset, ablate them, and measure (a) reduction in sycophantic agreement on held-out sycophancy probes vs. (b) collateral damage on general benchmarks (perplexity, simple QA). Test generalization across distinct sycophancy elicitation styles.

**Why it matters:** Sycophancy is a fuzzy-reward alignment failure that erodes oversight. A reproducible, surgical, training-free correction with measured side effects is valuable safety infrastructure independent of labs.

**Relevant context:** 'A Few Bad Neurons: Isolating and Surgically Correcting Sycophancy' (arXiv 2601.18939) isolates sycophancy in a few neurons. Open chat models (e.g. Qwen, Llama-3-8B-Instruct quantized) run on a single consumer GPU.
